listing_view.reasoning: No subscription, GMP, anchor, or peer data exists, so any listing call is a guess; but sellers asking ₹175-185 for a company whose profits never convert to cash (operating cash flow negative all three years, conversion vs PAT of -0.233) is a structurally fragile story once buyers look past the growth headline. The modest ₹1,682m issue size could still get engineered to list well, which is the only thing keeping this off the floor.

longterm_view.reasoning: Reported revenue grew ~61% CAGR and PAT ~72%, but none of it arrived as cash — operating cash flow was negative in all three years (₹-334m, ₹-7,654m, ₹-965m) and ~30% of incremental sales growth sat in uncollected receivables. The order book did roughly triple to ₹91,655 lakhs by July 2026 [business, page 207], which is real demand evidence, but a contractor that reports profit while burning cash must be funded continuously by someone, and this IPO is likely that funding.

governance.reasoning: The document affirmatively discloses no promoter benefits in the last two years and points to a related-party note [promoters, page 258], and claims no conflict of interest with suppliers [promoters, page 259]. These are the seller's own assertions and there is no red-flag disclosure visible, but also nothing independently verifiable — thin evidence in both directions.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Operating cash flow was negative every year while PAT grew 3x, meaning the earnings are accruals — receivables and contract assets, not money in the bank, and ~30% of sales growth is uncollected money.
With negative free cash flow in all three years (-₹434m, -₹7,713m, -₹1,522m) and wafer-thin net debt headroom, growth only continues while fresh capital keeps arriving.
Roughly 30 paise of every incremental rupee of sales is money the customer has not yet paid; in Indian EPC this is where write-offs and disputes hide.
The document itself flags that the sector has low entry barriers and is highly competitive, consistent with EBITDA margins stuck at 12.6-14.5% despite explosive growth.

answers.question: check whether the growth is organic and repeatable
answers.answer: Organic, plausibly — the order book rose from ₹39,139 lakhs to ₹68,743.52 lakhs and then ₹91,655 lakhs by July 31, 2026 [business, page 207], which is genuine demand, not acquisition accounting. But 'repeatable' is unproven: growth of this speed on negative operating cash flow is being bought with working capital, and it only repeats if collections improve or fresh money keeps coming in.

answers.question: veto — how is the business funded?
answers.answer: Not by its own operations: free cash flow is negative in all three years. The balance sheet shows negligible net debt (₹232m against ₹15,678m net worth) and net worth roughly tripled in two years, which is far more than retained profits can explain given no cash generation — so the growth has been funded by equity infusions or capital restructuring that I cannot fully reconstruct, and the IPO is the next tranche. That is a funding model built on continuous external capital, which fails my veto threshold.

answers.question: Our reading triggered a hard stop: negative operating cash flow in all three years. Is there an explanation in the document?
answers.answer: No extracted passage explains it. The order-book commentary attributes growth to credentials and execution [business, page 207] but says nothing about why operating cash flow was -₹334m, -₹7,654m, and -₹965m; the receivables build (29.6% of incremental sales) is the strongest implicit cause. The hard stop stands: the document, as given, reports three years of profits that never became cash and offers no reconciling explanation.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A cash-flow note showing FY2026 receivables actually collected after year-end, or customer concentration/advance-payment terms proving the receivables are short-cycle and contractual; without that, evidence that the working-capital intensity falls as the order book matures would soften the veto.
